name: Yaminawa
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 1 other work consulted does not discuss stress.
catalog_citation: Neely, Kelsey Caitlyn. 2019. The Linguistic Expression of Affective Stance in Yaminawa (Pano, Peru). PhD dissertation, University of California, Berkeley (eScholarship 8qs4w6sn; open copyhttps://core.ac.uk/download/484263901.pdf). Appendix C 'A sketch of Yaminawa grammar', §C.4.2 'Stress'
catalog_locator: Appendix C, §C.4.2 'Stress', pp. 257-258; tone/stress independence §C.4.5 'Tone', pp. 273-274 and §C.4 intro; variety identity §2.2.
catalog_quote: Primary stress in Yaminawa is word-initial. Metrical feet are left-aligned and iteratively trochaic, with no degenerate feet. Stress in Yaminawa is realized as an increase in vowel duration (vowels in stressed syllables are around 10-20 percent longer than vowels in unstressed syllables, as compared to long vowels (see section C.4.1 on lengthening of vowels in monosyllabic roots to meet the root bimoraicity requirement, which are around 50 percent longer than unstressed vowels). (117) a. (ˈbà.dì) 'leaf' ... c. (ˈbá.ʃá)ɾú 'jaguar' d. (ˈá.wá)(ˌwɨ̀.dà) 'butterfly' ... f. (ˈɨ́.kɨ̀ʂ)(ˌtì.ɾù)wù 'they may sew' ... Example (117f) demonstrates that initial stress is not weight-sensitive in Yaminawa. Example (117g) demonstrates that secondary stress is also weight-insensitive. It is not possible to demonstrate that long vowels do not attract stress as these vowels only occur word-initially, and always receive initial stress. ... A small number of nouns in Yaminawa have atypical stress patterns that are not predictable. All of these roots are three or more syllables and appear to be either loans or onomatopoetic forms.
world_status: statement found in an open source

new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first syllable of the word; the word is parsed into left-aligned syllabic trochees (σˈσ)(ˌσσ).., insensitive to syllable weight, so secondary stresses fall on the 3rd, 5th.. syllables; no degenerate feet (a final odd syllable is unfooted). Stress is cued by vowel duration. Yaminawa additionally has lexical tone (H, L, HL melodies, syllable = TBU), which Neely states does not interact with stress. Faust & Loos 2002 (SLP 51, p.18) independently agree on initial prominence: 'La primera sílaba de la frase nominal es tónica'; verb roots carry accent and high tone on the first syllable (intransitive) or first two syllables (transitive).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Iterative trochaic secondary stress on odd-numbered non-initial syllables, weight-insensitive, e.g. (ˈá.wá)(ˌwɨ.dà) 'butterfly', (ˈɨ.kɨʂ)(ˌtì.ɾù)wù 'they may sew', (ˈw̃ɨ.nã)(ˌmã.ɾìʃ)(ˌtá.kũ)ĩ; in verbs with trisyllabic reduplicants secondary stress impressionistically falls on the 4th syllable (first syllable of the base) instead.
new_statements.exceptions: A small set of 3+-syllable nouns, apparently loans or onomatopoeia, have unpredictable (final) stress: [ká.pí.ɾí.ˈbà] 'boquichico' (likely Yine loan), [tá.ká.ˈɾá] 'chicken'. Reduplicated verbs have irregular secondary stress. Monosyllabic verb roots lengthen to meet bimoraicity and always take initial stress, so attraction of stress by long vowels cannot be tested.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the (phonological) word; examples are citation forms of nouns and inflected verbs from the Río Sepahua dialect (ISO yaa) as spoken in Sepahua, Ucayali, Peru (Nahua/mts speakers also consulted). Tone is lexical and orthogonal to stress per the author. Note a genuine cross-source conflict: Brazilian descriptions of Jaminawa (Cruvinel 2013 MA, p.57) and of Saynáwa (Couto 2015, p.189) report FINAL primary stress; these are different communities in Acre (and Saynáwa's affiliation to Yaminawa is disputed), and neither analyses tone, so final H tone/phrase-final prominence may underlie the difference.
new_statements.identity_note: Primary statement (Neely 2019) describes the Río Sepahua dialect of Yaminawa (ISO yaa = yami1256) as spoken in Sepahua, Ucayali, Peru, with some Nahua (Yora, ISO mts, glottocode yora1241? -- Neely treats it under the blanket term Yaminawa) speakers consulted; Faust & Loos 2002 is also Peruvian Yaminahua (Purús/Yurúa SIL work). The Brazilian sources describe other communities of the Headwaters Nawa dialect complex: Cruvinel 2013 = 'Jaminawa do Brasil' (Acre: Assis Brasil, Mamoadate, Sena Madureira) and reports final stress; Couto 2015 = Saynáwa of T.I. Jamináwa do Igarapé Preto (Acre), a moribund variety whose membership in Yaminawa is disputed (Glottolog files it under yami1256 following Fleck 2013; Valenzuela & Guillaume place it in the Ucayali/Chama subgroup), also final stress. Catalog entry should be keyed to Peruvian Yaminawa (yaa) with the Brazilian discrepancy flagged.

tone_statements.citation: González, Carolina. 2017. Tipología de los sistemas métricos de veinticinco lenguas Pano. Amerindia 39(1): 129-172 (número temático 'Estudios sincrónicos y diacrónicos sobre lenguas Pano y Takana', eds. Pilar Valenzuela & Antoine Guillaume). Paris: A.E.A./CNRS-SeDyL.
tone_statements.quote: Otras lenguas Pano parecen ser trocaicas pero se necesita más investigación para esclarecer su sistema métrico. Entre ellas está el yaminahua, cuyo sistema acentual no está analizado por completo. Loos (2006) reporta que el acento principal recae normalmente en la primera sílaba de la palabra. Los correlatos del acento principal incluyen una mayor duración y, opcionalmente, una mayor amplitud (al menos en palabras de la forma CVCV). La altura tonal parece ser también un correlato (Loos 2006: 12; Faust & Loos 2002: 18). [...] Es posible que en otras lenguas cuya acentuación ha sido poco estudiada, como el yaminahua y el sharanawa, haya una distinción similar entre la asignación acentual y tonal.
tone_statements.translation: Other Panoan languages seem to be trochaic but more research is needed to clarify their metrical system. Among them is Yaminahua, whose stress system is not fully analysed. Loos (2006) reports that main stress normally falls on the first syllable of the word. The correlates of main stress include greater duration and, optionally, greater amplitude (at least in CVCV words). Pitch also seems to be a correlate (Loos 2006:12; Faust & Loos 2002:18). [...] It is possible that in other languages whose accentuation has been little studied, such as Yaminahua and Sharanawa, there is a similar distinction between stress assignment and tone assignment [as in Kashibo-Kakataibo].
tone_statements.locator: section 4 (end), p.151 including footnote 22 (the Yaminahua passage; not pp.151-152); section 7 'Discusión' (not 'Conclusiones'), p.164 (not p.166) for the stress/tone-split conjecture; Table 1, p.133 ('Yaminawa | 4 | Inicial | Trocaico (?) | Loos (2006)')
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)

sources.note: p.257: 'Primary stress in Yaminawa is word-initial. Metrical feet are left-aligned and iteratively trochaic, with no degenerate feet.' Stress realized as ~10-20% longer vowel; weight-insensitive (117f,g); secondary stress on odd syllables; a few 3+-syllable loans/onomatopoeia (kapiriˈba 'boquichico', takaˈra 'chicken') have unpredictable stress; reduplicated verbs impressionistically irregular in secondary stress. Language also has lexical tone (H, L, HL; TBU = syllable), p.273: 'There is no evidence for interactions between tone and stress.' Variety: Río Sepahua Yaminawa (yaa) + Nahua speake…

sources.note: Introducción, 'Fonología y símbolos ortográficos', p.18: 'No se escribe el acento. La raíz del verbo transitivo lleva acento y tono alto en las dos primeras sílabas. La raíz del verbo intransitivo lleva acento y tono alto únicamente en la primera sílaba. La primera sílaba de la frase nominal es tónica.' Repeated p.102-103 with examples [páké-] 'hacer caer' vs [páke-] 'caerse'; p.76 tonal pattern of disyllabic nouns diagnoses truncated third syllable. Accent and high tone are treated together; initial prominence.

sources.citation: Couto, Cláudio André Cavalcanti. 2015. A fonologia do Saynáwa (Pano): a língua falada pelos índios Saynáwa/Jamináwa da Terra Indígena Jamináwa do Igarapé Preto (Acre/Brasil). PhD, Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam. LOT Dissertation Series 414.
sources.note: Sec. 2.1.2, p.189-190: 'o acento primário é predizível na última sílaba das palavras.. revelando que o acento no Saynáwa não é morfológico'; primary stress on the final syllable regardless of weight, secondary stress on non-final heavy syllables ((C)VC, (C)V:) and on alternating light syllables in 4+ syllable words; metrical (Hayes 1995) analysis with Destressing in Clash. CAUTION: Saynáwa is a moribund variety whose affiliation is disputed (Fleck 2013 lists it as Yaminawa of Brazil; Valenzuela & Guillaume place it near Shipibo/Kapanawa; speakers reject the Jamináwa label) -- not a safe prima…

sources.citation: Cruvinel, Agmar Alves. 2013. Fonética e fonologia do Jaminawa do Brasil (Pano). MA thesis, Universidade Federal de Goiás. 93 pp.
sources.note: Sec. 4.3.1, p.57: 'nessa língua o acento sempre recai na última sílaba conforme acontece em outras línguas Pano como a Yawanawa (Paula, 2004) e a Shanenawa (Cândido 1998, 2004)'; weight-insensitive; in compounds primary stress final, first member keeps secondary stress. sources.note: Classes Yaminahua as (tentatively) trochaic with initial main stress whose correlates are duration, optionally amplitude, and apparently also pitch (citing Loos 2006:12 and Faust & Loos 2002:18, incl. the 'acento y tono alto' on the first two syllables of transitive roots vs first syllable of intransitives); in the conclusion suggests Yaminahua and Sharanawa may, like Kashibo-Kakataibo, have separate stress and tone assignment, but says the system is not fully analysed. Saynáwa is described as iambic with final stress (no tone).

tone.quote: Since Yaminahua word stress (in terms of amplitude, duration, or pitch) is usually, but not obligatorily, on the first syllable, it might at this point be a moot question whether it is the left edge of the stressed syllable or the left edge of the stem that the autosegment is associated to. The question naturally arises, Is stress defined by amplitude (loudness), duration, or pitch? I digress briefly to examine some stress data.
